doc.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998

title: Stressful playing situations: Philharmonic and Haydn concerto
summary: Wilder describes the tension of playing with the Philharmonic and doing the Haydn concerto, and Rowe and he discuss recovering from mistakes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Here’s another hard question. Can you recall some of the most difficult playing situations you’ve been in, just from a trumpet standpoint? And did you get through them successfully?

A couple of times when I played with the Philharmonic, and it wasn’t difficult but I found it to be a little stressful because here you’re somebody who is not really generally playing in that idiom and now you’re in the middle of it and you’ve got to perform like everybody else, and I found that a little tensing. But it’s rewarding of course to do it, and I was very flattered, because how often does anybody who’s supposed to be a commercial or a jazz player get an opportunity to do something like that. It was totally unrelated to the other things that I’d been accustomed to doing. But then there’ve been some other situations, I did the Haydn “Trumpet Concerto” a few times with the Municipal Concerts Orchestra in New York. And I did it with the ABC Symphony once. And in doing some of those things of course you can’t help but feel a little tension. But again, it’s challenging and once having done it, it’s very rewarding.
The definition of a mistake is much clearer in that music. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-

I mean I noticed a few times in the Fallcoming concert we just heard, which was great, that there was a few times that I think the soloist may have gone in a direction that they didn’t really intend, but you’re able to —
You’re able to get around that.
Get around it and get out of it, and it sounded like you meant to do it, whether or not you did.
Right. That’s when your faculties come into focus, and again trying to — you create something that you didn’t intend to create. And it comes off, very often.
